chapter_title: The Human is less than all the Things of the Universe, and he is rebellious beyond them all.
chapter_note: This chapter contains no extractable cosmological-correspondential substrate. It is entirely composed of later layers: apostolic narrative (Mani at a river-bed), Manichaean theological argument (humanity's rebellion, anti-monotheist theodicy), dialogue framing, and two catechetical lists that Gardner notes 'appear to have been added to the text.' The theological argument — that mountains and seas are silent before God while humanity blasphemes by attributing evil to God — is a distinctive Manichaean doctrinal position, not systematic correspondential mapping. The five things Jesus revealed (P8-12) and three things the faithful live by (P14-16) are catechetical summaries that REFERENCE cosmological content without EXPOUNDING it. Teaching purity is only 0.200, confirming the near-absence of substrate vocabulary.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Apostolic narrative: Mani traveling and arriving at a river-bed. Matches institutional layer definition of 'Mani's calling, journeys, encounters.' Bridge connective 'Furthermore' links to prior chapter. No cosmological mapping — purely biographical scene-setting.

Continuation of apostolic narrative. Mani's speech comparing humanity ('five words of the flesh') to a mountain. Heavily damaged text. The comparison is rhetorical/homiletic, not systematic correspondence. 'Five words of the flesh' may reference a five-fold classification of living beings but the framing is entirely apostolic teaching narrative.

Seam flag fires but is somewhat misleading — this continues the same apostolic narrative, not extending a substrate sequence. The argument that mountains and seas exist in silence and do not blaspheme God is Manichaean theodicy. 'Good works of righteousness' and 'cause of evil' are theological-institutional vocabulary. 'The power that supports the totality' has cosmological resonance but is used within theological argument, not domain mapping.

Core of the Manichaean theodicy argument: humanity blasphemes by attributing evil beings (rulers, demons, fiends, satans) to God. 'The idol of ill-fated humanity' is a Manichaean theological characterization. The polemic against those who say evil comes from God is distinctly Manichaean anti-monotheist positioning, not pre-Mani cosmological teaching.

Pure dialogue frame: narrative transition ('when he had recounted this') + disciple speaks + generic request ('Tell us, our master, and instruct us about this lesson'). No substantive cosmological question — just a request to explain further. High dialogue_frame score (17.65) confirms.

Disciple's substantive question, but about Christology, not cosmology: why did Jesus come if humanity doesn't belong to God? References Jesus as 'son of the Living God,' crucifixion, persecution, torment — all Manichaean Christological narrative. The question reveals Manichaean theological structure, not pre-Mani cosmological structure.

Mani's answer about Jesus's multiple roles: cosmological task 'outside in the great universe,' revelation to Adam and Eve, sending apostles 'generation by generation.' This is Manichaean salvation history. Even the cosmological reference ('his task outside in the great universe') is a summary, not systematic teaching. 'He sent the apostles' is institutional succession narrative.

First of five catechetical points: 'they belong to the race of light.' Gardner notes these lists appear to have been added. This is a catechetical summary — it REFERENCES the light/dark cosmology without EXPOUNDING it through systematic mapping.

Second catechetical point: knowledge of 'aeons of the greatness' and 'the manner of the darkness.' The cosmological content is REFERENCED ('how they occur,' 'how it too exists') but not TAUGHT. The frame is 'He unveiled/taught them about X' — a catechetical summary of teaching, not the teaching itself.
Third catechetical point: light conquered darkness. Again references cosmological content ('the light greatness... against the power of darkness') without systematic exposition. Catechetical summary.

Fourth catechetical point: descent to 'the province of death,' flesh, rescue from 'the gate of the underworld.' Contains cosmological geography vocabulary but in catechetical summary form. Soteriological narrative, not cosmological mapping.

Fifth catechetical point: rebels bound in a fetter. 'The righteousness that is proclaimed by the apostle' — explicitly institutional, referencing the apostle's proclamation. Eschatological summary, not substrate.

'Once again the apostle speaks' is dialogue_frame formula, but it introduces purely institutional content: 'All the faithful who believe this truth shall live by three great mighty things.' Since the substantive content is institutional (the faithful, belief, catechetical enumeration), classifying as institutional. The frame formula is noted but does not warrant mixed classification when no substrate is present to extract.

First of three catechetical points: 'counted to the race of faith and truth, this living one that enlightens.' Institutional community identity language — being counted to the faithful race. No cosmological mapping.

Second catechetical point: 'received the right hand and the peace from above' and 'believed the apostle who has been manifested.' 'Right hand and peace' is ritual/institutional language. 'The apostle who has been manifested' is explicit institutional reference.

Third catechetical point: 'act with restraint and charity to the Cross of Light.' The Cross of Light 'which grieves in the totality, being present in what is visible and what is not visible' contains cosmological vocabulary (substrate score 10.34) — this is the Jesus patibilis concept. However, the cosmological description is a subordinate clause within a catechetical instruction about ethical behavior. The paragraph's function is prescriptive (how the faithful should act), not expository (how the cosmos is structured). The cosmological fragment serves the catechetical frame, not the reverse.
